---
title: "Quantum Circuits — Operations First, Measurement Last"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

What happens when a Hadamard gate is followed by another Hadamard gate on |0⟩? Many beginners expect two random outcomes, but there is only one final measurement.

## The core concept

The amplitudes can interfere. Intermediate operations are not necessarily observations. Two Hadamard gates reverse one another on an isolated qubit.

## Express it mathematically

$$
H^2|0\rangle=I|0\rangle=|0\rangle
$$

**Every symbol explained:** H² means apply Hadamard twice; I is the identity operation that leaves a state unchanged; |0⟩ is the original and final state.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Start from amplitude vector [1,0]. After the first H, get [1/√2,1/√2]. After the second H, the first component becomes (1/√2+1/√2)/√2=1; the second becomes (1/√2−1/√2)/√2=0. A final measurement returns 0 with 100% probability ideally.

## Why it works

This is interference: relative amplitudes may reinforce or cancel. A circuit works by composing operators before measurement, and the ordering of gates is significant when gates do not commute.

## Go one level deeper

On noisy hardware two H gates may still yield some 1 outcomes due to imperfect gates and measurements. Sampling outcomes from a real device differs from exact statevector simulation.

## Common misunderstanding

Quantum speedup does not follow merely from using qubits; algorithms need structure that turns interference into useful answer probabilities.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
